contributions: the Long CoT Collection, a 100K-example dataset generated by short-CoT LLMs (not distilled from a long-reasoning model's raw output) via a reasoning-flow-guided, step-by-step generation pipeline
a demonstration that this dataset is a reliable, 2-3x more effective RL cold-start than the base model on MATH500/GPQA under RLVR, addressing sparse-reward instability

built-in controllability over the target thought budget during dataset construction, offered as a mechanism for managing overthinking (generating an unnecessarily large number of tokens for simple problems), with an empirical showing that reducing budget too aggressively (25%) both shortens and degrades reasoning quality
datasets: Long CoT Collection (new, 100K instances, three thought-budget variants at 100%/50%/25%)
limitations: The construction pipeline was validated only using o1 as the single reference teacher LRM; extending it to other partially-disclosed-reasoning LRMs is left to future work. Phase 2 (the RL cold-start experiment) uses only a 0.5B model due to GPU resource constraints (16 A100 40GB GPUs), so whether the 2-3x RLVR gain holds at larger scales is untested, even though Phase 1 SFT experiments use 7-8B models. The pipeline is validated on math and general reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, AIME2024, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro); the paper explicitly flags applying it to expert/specialized domains as future work.
method: First collects a 1K seed dataset by manually gathering o1's reference reasoning flow (an outline sequence of reasoning steps) and thought budget (thought-token count, from the OpenAI API's total-minus-response token difference) for questions from the magpie-reasoning-V1 dataset. Then, for 100K new questions, retrieves the most relevant seed demonstration by domain match and thought-budget match, has GPT-4o (a short-CoT LLM) generate an analogous reasoning-flow outline for the new question guided by the retrieved demonstration, then generates the long CoT rationale step-by-step (one rationale per outline step, conditioned on prior rationales and the next outline step), and finally filters out rationales that reach a wrong final answer (validated by GPT-4o against the ground-truth answer), keeping 76% of generated instances. The retrieval/generation pipeline is thought-budget-controllable: constructing three dataset variants at 100%, 50% and 25% of the reference thought budget by constraining the number of reasoning outlines used.
one_liner: Introduces the Long CoT Collection, a 100K-example dataset built by having short-CoT LLMs (GPT-4o) generate o1-style long reasoning traces from a 1K seed of teacher-annotated reasoning flow and thought-budget targets, showing it is a stronger RL cold-start than the base model (2-3x larger RLVR gains) and offers built-in controllability over thought budget to address overthinking.
problem: Building open long-CoT SFT datasets to cold-start RL training of large reasoning models has relied on directly distilling completions from an existing closed long-reasoning model (o1) or its open replica (R1), leaving the actual mechanism for constructing such data from scratch unclear and keeping the field dependent on existing LRMs.

relevance.overthinking: Directly relevant and self-identified: the paper explicitly names overthinking ('generating an unnecessarily large number of tokens for simple problems') as a major LRM issue and positions the dataset's thought-budget controllability as a mechanism to address it -- the 25%-budget ablation (Table 2) is direct evidence that cutting thought budget too aggressively during training data construction degrades downstream reasoning quality, a concrete data point on the cost side of the length-vs-accuracy tradeoff that overthinking mitigation methods must navigate, here approached from the data-construction stage rather than inference-time control.

results: Head-to-head comparison (o3-mini as judge, 100 questions with correct R1 answers) shows the collection's rationales win on Reasoning Flow quality (63% win vs. 37% for R1) but lose on Strategy (41% win vs. 51% for R1, 8% tie) and mostly tie/lose on Correctness (9% win, 75% tie, 16% lose vs. R1) -- described as 'competitive' with R1 despite being generated by a short-CoT model. Best-of-N sampling (Pass@N, N=1..32) on MATH500 and AIME2024 shows models SFT'd on the collection (Llama-3.1-8B-LC, Qwen2.5-7B-LC) improve over their un-tuned base models across N, with Qwen2.5-7B-LC's advantage growing at large N (16, 32) while the base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's performance saturates -- interpreted as the collection enabling more diverse response exploration useful for RL. On GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro, models trained on the collection show gains, e.g. Qwen2.5-7B-LC's GPQA Diamond (44.5) slightly exceeds Bespoke-7B (a simpler R1-distillation replica, 38.9) using open weights and open data; Llama-3.1-8B-LC improves over its base (43.7 to 44.5 on MMLU-Pro). The main RL result: initializing a Qwen2.5-0.5B policy by SFT on the Long CoT Collection before RLVR (GRPO with length/answer/format rewards) yields 2-3x larger accuracy gains from RLVR than starting RL directly from the base Qwen2.5-0.5B, on both MATH500 (+13.3pp vs. +5.4pp) and GPQA (+11.5pp vs. +5.6pp) -- addressing the RL cold-start instability problem. Thought-budget analysis shows the collection's reasoning-trigger phrase usage (e.g. 'Let's,' 'Wait,' 'Verify-') sits between GPT-4o's minimal use and DeepSeek-R1's extensive use, and reducing the target thought budget to 25% degrades downstream MATH500 accuracy (66.6 -> 60.7 -> 57.6 across 100%/50%/25% budget variants) and produces confusing rationales when the outline count is cut too aggressively relative to content.
